title: The Book of Lamentations
lead: Five poems of grief for Jerusalem after the Babylonian conquest of 586 BC: four of them alphabet poems, voiced by a narrator, the city as a woman, a suffering man and the whole community, and read by Jews every year on the Ninth of Av.

sections.b: Lamentations has five chapters. Chapters 1 and 2 are alphabet poems of 22 verses with three lines each; chapter 3 has 66 verses, three to each letter; chapter 4 is an alphabet poem of 22 two-line verses; chapter 5 has 22 verses but no alphabet. The speakers are a narrator, Daughter Zion, a man who has seen affliction and the community. The book names no author and no person. The Hebrew title is the first word, 'eikhah, "How!"; the Talmud calls it Qinot, "Laments"; Greek and Latin Bibles call it "Dirges", and they place it after Jeremiah because of the tradition that he wrote it.
sections.refs: Lamentations 1:1; Lamentations 2:1; Lamentations 3:1; Lamentations 4:1; Lamentations 5:1; 2 Chronicles 35:25

sections.b: In the Hebrew Bible Lamentations is one of the Five Scrolls in the Writings and is read on the Ninth of Av. In the Latin church the traditional Office of Tenebrae takes its lessons from Lamentations on the last days of Holy Week, and composers from Palestrina and Tallis to Stravinsky have set it. Its most quoted lines, "The LORD's acts of loyal love have not ended" and "your faithfulness is great", come from the middle of chapter 3.

sections.h: A book with no happy ending
sections.b: The book ends with a question about whether God has rejected his people (Lamentations 5:22). Jewish custom repeats the verse before it, a prayer for return, so that the reading does not end on that note. Modern readers ask whether the open ending is the book's point.
